knitr::opts_chunk$set(

library(mvgam)

theme_set(mvgam_theme(base_size = 12, base_family = "serif"))

Do the plankton of a lake regulate one another from month to month,
or do they rise and fall with the same seasons and nutrients? A
vector autoregression (VAR) separates the two. It lets the state of
each taxon this month depend on the state of every taxon last month.
The coefficients of that dependence form a matrix $A$. Its
off-diagonal cells are the lagged interactions between taxa
(Lütkepohl [2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-27752-1)).

mvgam fits the VAR to latent states. Because each measurement
carries observation error of its own (Auger-Méthé et al.
[2021](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1470)), a separate observation
model links those states to the data. This article fits that
model to five plankton taxa from Lake Washington, then works through
what a fitted VAR offers: the interactions in $A$, the correlation
of the taxa's shocks, impulse responses, variance decompositions,
stability metrics and forecasts.

## The data

The MARSS package (Holmes et al.
[2012](https://doi.org/10.32614/RJ-2012-002)) distributes monthly
plankton densities and water conditions for Lake Washington from
1962 to 1994, drawn from the long-term monitoring of W. T. Edmondson.
In the transformed version each density is log-transformed and then
z-scored over the whole record, with zero counts recorded as missing.

We use the fifteen years from 1980 to 1994. That window is long
enough to estimate monthly interactions and short enough to fit in
minutes. We use five taxa. Four are
groups of phytoplankton: diatoms, green algae, unicellular algae and
the cryptophyte *Cryptomonas*. The fifth is *Daphnia*, a grazing
zooplankter that eats them. Two water conditions enter as
covariates. Temperature has a strong seasonal cycle. Because a smooth
of month describes that cycle, the covariate is the temperature
anomaly, each month's temperature less the mean for its calendar
month. Phosphorus income controlled the growth of algae in
Lake Washington (Edmondson and Lehman
[1981](https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.1981.26.1.0001)). Total
phosphorus averaged over the twelve months to each month measures
that nutrient loading.

```{r data}
load(url("https://github.com/atsa-es/MARSS/raw/master/data/lakeWAplankton.rda"))
lake <- as.data.frame(lakeWAplanktonTrans)
lake$TP_annual <- as.numeric(
  stats::filter(lake$TP, rep(1 / 12, 12), sides = 1)
)
lake <- lake[lake$Year >= 1980, ]
lake$time <- seq_len(nrow(lake))
lake$temp_anom <- lake$Temp - ave(lake$Temp, lake$Month)

taxa <- c("Diatoms", "Greens", "Unicells", "Cryptomonas", "Daphnia")
plankton <- do.call(rbind, lapply(taxa, function(taxon) {
  data.frame(
    y = lake[[taxon]], time = lake$time, year = lake$Year,
    month = lake$Month, temp_anom = lake$temp_anom,
    TP_annual = lake$TP_annual, series = taxon
  )
}))
plankton$series <- factor(plankton$series, levels = taxa)
```

The data are in long format, one row per taxon and month. `series`
names the taxon and `time` counts the months. The order of the
levels of `series` fixes the order of the taxa in every output
below. We hold 1994 out to score forecasts against:

```{r split}
train <- plankton[plankton$year < 1994, ]
test <- plankton[plankton$year == 1994, ]
```

`mvgam_data()` checks the data against the model's requirements and
plots each series, with the held-out months marked:

```{r plot-data, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Monthly log densities of the five taxa, z-scored over 1962 to 1994. The final year is held out."}
mvgam_data(train, family = gaussian(), newdata = test)
```

Each taxon cycles through the seasons. The unicellular algae also
decline from 1980 until about 1988 and then level off, with two
brief collapses near the end of the decline. A seasonal model alone
would miss that decline.

## The model

The model has two layers. The observation layer says that each
log density $y_{s,t}$ measures a latent state $x_{s,t}$ with
observation error, whose standard deviation $\sigma_s$ differs by
taxon:

$$
y_{s,t} \sim \mathrm{Normal}(x_{s,t},\ \sigma_s).
$$

The latent state is a mean set by the covariates plus a deviation
$z_{s,t}$ that follows the VAR:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{s,t} &= \alpha_s + \beta_s\,\mathrm{TP}_t
  + \gamma_s\,\mathrm{temp}_t + f_s(\mathrm{month}_t) + z_{s,t}, \\
\mathbf{z}_t &\sim \mathrm{MVN}(A\,\mathbf{z}_{t-1},\ \Sigma).
\end{aligned}
$$

Each taxon has its own level $\alpha_s$ and seasonal smooth $f_s$,
with its own slopes on phosphorus loading and on the temperature
anomaly. $A$ holds the lagged effects among the deviations. $\Sigma$
holds the covariance of the monthly shocks. The VAR describes how
taxa push one another away from their seasonal and nutrient-driven
means. Seasonality itself stays out of $A$.

mvgam's `VAR()` keeps the process stationary: after a disturbance,
every deviation returns towards zero. The prior on $A$ enforces this
(Heaps [2023](https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2022.2079648)). A
stationary VAR cannot absorb a slow drift in a taxon's mean. When we
fitted the model without phosphorus, the four chains disagreed about
the level of the unicellular algae, whose decline nothing in that
model explained.
The phosphorus slope gives the drift a cause outside the VAR.

The observation and process variances both describe scatter around
the same latent state. Fourteen years of data from one lake separate
them poorly: a month's departure could be observation error or real
change. The prior on $\log\sigma_s$ supplies the missing
information. We centred it on $\log 0.25$ with a standard deviation
of $0.2$, which places observation error near a quarter of a standard
deviation of log density, below the change in the populations from
month to month. The data still move each taxon's observation standard
deviation away from that prior.

In mvgam the trend formula holds the latent model. `lv_axis()` gives
a term a separate effect for each taxon. `bf()` gives the
observation standard deviation a formula of its own. With
`sigma ~ 0 + series`, it takes one value per taxon. The observation
formula `y ~ -1` adds nothing to the latent state.

```{r fit}
fit <- mvgam(
  formula = bf(y ~ -1, sigma ~ 0 + series),
  trend_formula = ~ lv_axis() + TP_annual:lv_axis() +
    temp_anom:lv_axis() + s(month, by = lv_axis(), bs = "cc", k = 5) +
    VAR(cor = TRUE),
  family = gaussian(),
  data = train,
  newdata = test,
  knots = list(month = c(0.5, 12.5)),
  priors = prior(normal(-1.4, 0.2), class = b, dpar = sigma),
  chains = 4,
  iter = 1500,
  warmup = 750,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95),
  seed = 1980,
  silent = 2
)
```

`bs = "cc"` makes each seasonal smooth cyclic. December then joins
January, at the boundary that `knots` places between them.
`cor = TRUE` estimates the correlations among the shocks in
$\Sigma$. Passing `newdata` stores the held-out year on the model
for forecasting. `seed` makes the sampling reproducible.

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
# Format an estimate with its interval for inline reporting
ci <- function(est, lo, hi, digits = 2) {
  # A value that rounds to zero prints without a minus sign
  f <- function(v) sub("^-(0\\.0+)$", "\\1",
                       formatC(v, format = "f", digits = digits))
  paste0(f(est), " [", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), "]")
}
```

## Checking the fit

We first checked that the model reproduces the data. `pp_check()`
draws replicate data sets from the posterior and overlays their
densities on the observed one, here separately for each taxon:

```{r ppc, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Density of the observed values (dark line) and of 50 replicate data sets drawn from the posterior (light lines), one panel per taxon."}
pp_check(fit, type = "dens_overlay_grouped", group = "series",
         ndraws = 50)
```

The simulated densities bracket the observed density of every taxon.
They reproduce the two peaks of *Daphnia*, which spends winter scarce
and summer abundant.

## What sets the means

The covariates and seasonal smooths give each taxon's expected log
density when no taxon deviates from its mean. `fixef()` with
`trend_effects = TRUE` reports the coefficients of the trend formula:

```{r fixef}
round(fixef(fit, trend_effects = TRUE), 2)
```

```{r fixef-numbers, include = FALSE}
fe <- fixef(fit, trend_effects = TRUE)
fx <- function(term) {
  row <- paste0(term, "_trend")
  ci(fe[row, "Estimate"], fe[row, "Q2.5"], fe[row, "Q97.5"])
}
fe_tp_uni <- fx("seriesUnicells:TP_annual")
fe_temp_dia <- fx("seriesDiatoms:temp_anom")
```

Because total phosphorus fell across the record, the positive slope
of the unicellular algae on phosphorus predicts the decline the first
figure shows. Their slope is `r fe_tp_uni` standard deviations of log
density per unit of phosphorus. The intervals of the other four phosphorus slopes span
zero.

mvgam computes effects on the outcome scale through the
marginaleffects package (Arel-Bundock et al.
[2024](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v111.i09)). Every call here
passes `type = "expected"`, which predicts the expected log density
$E[y]$ and leaves observation error out of the interval drawn around
it. The marginaleffects default, `type = "response"`, draws new
observations with their observation error. A contrast between two
such predictions carries that error twice. Slopes and comparisons
come from the expected log density under either setting.
`avg_slopes()` averages the
slope of the expected log density over the data, here separately for
each taxon:

```{r slopes}
marginaleffects::avg_slopes(fit, variables = "TP_annual",
                            by = "series", type = "expected")
```

In a Gaussian model with an identity link, each slope has the
posterior of its coefficient. The table reports medians, where
`fixef()` reports means. Under a nonlinear link they differ. `avg_slopes()`
then reports the change on the outcome scale, which the coefficients
do not give directly. `conditional_effects()` draws each effect with
the other covariates held at their means:

```{r ce-tp, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Expected log density against twelve-month total phosphorus for each taxon, with 95% credible intervals."}
conditional_effects(fit, effects = "TP_annual", type = "expected")
```

The seasonal smooths carry the cycle that dominated the data plot:

```{r ce-month, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Seasonal smooths of expected log density by calendar month, with 95% credible intervals."}
conditional_effects(fit, effects = "month", type = "expected")
```

Diatoms peak in spring and reach their low in autumn. Green algae and
*Daphnia* peak in mid-summer. *Cryptomonas* peaks in April. The
temperature anomaly adds little once season is in the model. Its
largest slope, for the diatoms, is `r fe_temp_dia`.

## Interactions among the taxa

`posterior_transition_matrix()` summarises the transition matrix
cell by cell. Row $i$, column $j$ is the effect of taxon $j$'s deviation last
month on taxon $i$'s deviation this month:

```{r A}
A <- posterior_transition_matrix(fit)
A
```

```{r A-numbers, include = FALSE}
cell <- function(i, j) ci(A$A[i, j], A$A_lower[i, j], A$A_upper[i, j])
fe_a_dc <- cell("Cryptomonas", "Daphnia")
fe_a_cd <- cell("Daphnia", "Cryptomonas")
fe_a_dia <- cell("Diatoms", "Cryptomonas")
fe_a_cd_pos <- sprintf("%.0f%%",
                       100 * A$prob_positive["Daphnia", "Cryptomonas"])
fe_a_diag <- sprintf("%.2f", range(diag(A$A)))
clear <- A$A_lower > 0 | A$A_upper < 0
diag(clear) <- FALSE
n_clear <- sum(clear)
more_fewer <- function(x) if (x < 0) "fewer" else "more"
dc_word <- more_fewer(A$A["Cryptomonas", "Daphnia"])
dia_word <- more_fewer(A$A["Diatoms", "Cryptomonas"])
```

The diagonal describes persistence. Each taxon's deviation carries a
coefficient between `r fe_a_diag[1]` and `r fe_a_diag[2]` into the
next month. The heatmap outlines each cell whose
95% interval excludes zero:

```{r plot-A, fig.width = 6, fig.asp = 0.8, fig.cap = "Posterior mean of the transition matrix. Rows are the taxa at month t and columns the taxa at month t - 1. Outlined cells have 95% credible intervals that exclude zero."}
plot(A)
```

In this fit, `r n_clear` of the twenty off-diagonal cells clear zero.
Two cells have an ecological interpretation. The first is grazing. A month
with more *Daphnia* than expected is followed by `r dc_word`
*Cryptomonas*, with a coefficient of `r fe_a_dc`. The effect of
*Cryptomonas* on *Daphnia* is `r fe_a_cd`. It is positive in
`r fe_a_cd_pos` of the posterior draws, which suggests that more food
in one month brings more grazers in the next. Fourteen years of
monthly data do not settle that effect.

The second cell links *Cryptomonas* to the diatoms. A month with more
*Cryptomonas* than expected is followed by `r dia_word` diatoms, with
a coefficient of `r fe_a_dia`. Because no feeding link runs between
two phytoplankton groups, the likelier source is a driver the model
omits, such as a change in mixing that favours one group before the
other. A coefficient in $A$ records that one deviation predicts
another without naming a mechanism.

## Shocks and states

The transition matrix describes how taxa push one another over time.
The innovation covariance $\Sigma$ describes which taxa receive the
same unmodelled push in the same month. A change in light or mixing
that the covariates miss would appear as a correlation between the
shocks of the taxa it affects. `residual_cor()` with
`covariance = "innovation"` reports these correlations:

```{r rc-innov}
rc_innov <- residual_cor(fit, covariance = "innovation")
summary(rc_innov)
```

```{r rc-numbers, include = FALSE}
pair <- function(rc, a, b) {
  s <- summary(rc)
  r <- s[(s$series_1 == a & s$series_2 == b) |
           (s$series_1 == b & s$series_2 == a), ]
  ci(r$Estimate, r$Q_lower, r$Q_upper)
}
fe_i_uc <- pair(rc_innov, "Unicells", "Cryptomonas")
fe_i_cd <- pair(rc_innov, "Cryptomonas", "Daphnia")
```

The shocks of the unicellular algae and *Cryptomonas* correlate most
strongly, at `r fe_i_uc`. The model holds no covariate that would explain the shared rise.

The default, `covariance = "stationary"`, correlates the deviations
themselves. Each deviation accumulates the shocks of many months,
passed through $A$:

```{r rc-stat, fig.width = 6, fig.asp = 0.8, fig.cap = "Posterior mean correlations among the deviations of the five taxa. Outlined pairs have 95% credible intervals that exclude zero."}
rc <- residual_cor(fit)
plot(rc)
```

```{r rc-stat-numbers, include = FALSE}
fe_s_uc <- pair(rc, "Unicells", "Cryptomonas")
fe_s_cd <- pair(rc, "Cryptomonas", "Daphnia")
```

The two correlations differ where $A$ couples the taxa. The shocks of
*Cryptomonas* and *Daphnia* correlate at `r fe_i_cd`. Their
deviations correlate at `r fe_s_cd`. Grazing passes each shock to the
other taxon over the following months, which changes the correlation
the shared shocks create. $A$ barely couples the unicellular algae and
*Cryptomonas*. Their correlations are `r fe_i_uc` for the shocks and
`r fe_s_uc` for the deviations.

## Impulse responses

An impulse response gives the expected path of every taxon after a
single shock to one of them (Lütkepohl
[2005](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-27752-1)). `irf()` computes
the generalised impulse response by default (Pesaran and Shin
[1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0165-1765(97)00214-0)). The shock to
one taxon brings with it the shocks that its correlated taxa receive
in the same month, in the proportions $\Sigma$ implies. Horizon 1 is
the month of the shock.

```{r irf}
irfs <- irf(fit, h = 12)
```

`plot()` with `series = 5` draws the responses to a shock in the
fifth taxon, *Daphnia*:

```{r plot-irf, fig.asp = 0.75, fig.cap = "Generalised impulse responses of each taxon to a one standard deviation shock in Daphnia, with 95% credible intervals. Horizon 1 is the month of the shock."}
plot(irfs, series = 5)
```

```{r irf-numbers, include = FALSE}
ir <- as.data.frame(irfs)
resp <- function(shock, h) {
  r <- ir[ir$shock == shock & ir$horizon == h, ]
  ci(r$irfQ50, r$irfQ2.5, r$irfQ97.5)
}
fe_ir_dd1 <- resp("Daphnia -> Daphnia", 1)
fe_ir_dc1 <- resp("Daphnia -> Cryptomonas", 1)
fe_ir_dc3 <- resp("Daphnia -> Cryptomonas", 3)
fe_ir_du2 <- resp("Daphnia -> Unicells", 2)
own_d <- ir[ir$shock == "Daphnia -> Daphnia", ]
h_dd <- own_d$horizon[which(abs(own_d$irfQ50) < 0.05)[1]]
fe_dd_decay <- if (is.na(h_dd)) {
  "The rise stays above 0.05 through month twelve."
} else {
  paste0("The rise falls below 0.05 by month ", h_dd, ".")
}
from_daphnia <- ir[startsWith(ir$shock, "Daphnia ->"), ]
settled <- vapply(seq_len(12), function(h) {
  all(abs(from_daphnia$irfQ50[from_daphnia$horizon >= h]) < 0.01)
}, logical(1))
fe_settle <- if (any(settled)) {
  paste0("Every response stays within 0.01 of zero from month ",
         which(settled)[1], ".")
} else {
  "Some responses stay above 0.01 at month twelve."
}
```

A shock raises *Daphnia* by `r fe_ir_dd1` in its first month.
`r fe_dd_decay` Because the shocks of *Daphnia* and *Cryptomonas* are
correlated, *Cryptomonas* moves with *Daphnia* in the first month, by
`r fe_ir_dc1`. Grazing then acts through $A$. In the third month
*Cryptomonas* is at `r fe_ir_dc3` relative to its expected level. The
unicellular algae change by `r fe_ir_du2` in the second month.
`r fe_settle`

## Variance decompositions

A forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD) splits the variance of
each taxon's forecast among the taxa whose shocks generate it, at
each horizon. `fevd()` splits the variance with the Cholesky factor
of $\Sigma$, taken in the order of the levels of `series`. Where the
shocks of two taxa correlate, the factor assigns the shared part to
whichever taxon comes first. The diatoms come first and keep all of
their own shock.

```{r fevd, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.6, fig.cap = "Median share of each taxon's forecast error variance that each source of shocks generates, by forecast horizon. Panels are the taxa forecast. Colours are the taxa whose shocks generate the variance."}
fevds <- fevd(fit, h = 12)
plot(fevds)
```

```{r fevd-numbers, include = FALSE}
fv <- as.data.frame(fevds)
share <- function(shock, h) {
  r <- fv[fv$shock == shock & fv$horizon == h, ]
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r$fevdQ50)
}
fe_fv_uc1 <- share("Unicells -> Cryptomonas", 1)
fe_fv_uc12 <- share("Unicells -> Cryptomonas", 12)
fe_fv_cd12 <- share("Cryptomonas -> Daphnia", 12)
own <- vapply(strsplit(fv$shock, " -> ", fixed = TRUE),
              function(s) s[1] == s[2], logical(1))
others <- own & fv$horizon == 12 &
  fv$shock != "Cryptomonas -> Cryptomonas"
fe_fv_own <- sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * range(fv$fevdQ50[others]))
```

For every taxon but *Cryptomonas*, its own shocks generate most of
its forecast variance. At twelve months those own shares run from
`r fe_fv_own[1]` to `r fe_fv_own[2]`. For *Cryptomonas*, the unicellular
algae generate `r fe_fv_uc1` of its forecast variance in the first
month and `r fe_fv_uc12` by month twelve. Most of that share comes
from the correlation of the two taxa's shocks. The ordering assigns
it to the unicellular algae because they come first. The coupling of
the two taxa appears in the *Daphnia* panel, where *Cryptomonas* shocks generate
`r fe_fv_cd12` of the twelve-month forecast variance. Reordering the
levels of `series` and refitting would move the shared part of each
correlated pair to the other taxon. The generalised impulse responses
above are the same in any order.

## Stability of the community

`stability()` summarises the dynamics in $A$ as community stability
metrics (Ives et al.
[2003](https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9615(2003)073[0301:ECSAEI]2.0.CO;2)).
Reactivity is the log of the largest singular value of $A$. Above
zero, some perturbation grows in the month after it occurs before the
community returns towards its means (Neubert et al.
[2009](https://doi.org/10.1890/08-2014.1)). The mean return rate is
the largest modulus of the eigenvalues of $A$. Once the slowest mode
dominates, the distance from the means shrinks by about this factor
each month. The variance return rate is its square. It describes how
fast the forecast variance settles.

```{r stability, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.4, fig.cap = "Posterior distributions of reactivity and of the mean and variance return rates. The dashed line marks zero reactivity."}
stab <- stability(fit)
plot(stab)
```

```{r stability-numbers, include = FALSE}
st <- function(m) {
  r <- stab[stab$metric == m, ]
  ci(r$Estimate, r$Q2.5, r$Q97.5)
}
fe_react <- st("reactivity")
fe_react_neg <- sprintf(
  "%.0f%%",
  100 * mean(stability(fit, summary = FALSE)$reactivity < 0)
)
fe_mrr <- st("mean_return_rate")
mrr <- stab$Estimate[stab$metric == "mean_return_rate"]
fe_half <- sprintf("%.1f", log(0.5) / log(mrr))
```

Reactivity is `r fe_react`, with `r fe_react_neg` of the posterior
below zero. The data favour a community that damps every
perturbation from the first month. They do not exclude one that
briefly amplifies some perturbations. The mean return rate is
`r fe_mrr`. At the median, a deviation halves in about `r fe_half`
months. The plankton community returns to its seasonal and
nutrient-driven means within a season.

## Forecasting the held-out year

Passing `newdata` at fitting stored 1994 on the model. `forecast()`
projects the fitted states forward through those twelve months and
adds observation error:

```{r forecast, fig.width = 8, fig.asp = 0.6, fig.cap = "Fitted values to the end of 1993 and forecasts for 1994 (right of the dashed line), with observations as points."}
fc <- forecast(fit)
plot(fc)
```

`score()` compares the forecast distributions with the 1994
observations. The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures
the distance between a forecast distribution and the observation, in
the units of the data. Lower is better. `in_interval` records whether
the observation fell inside the 90% forecast interval:

```{r score}
sc <- score(fc, score = "crps")
data.frame(
  taxon = taxa,
  mean_crps = vapply(taxa, function(t) mean(sc[[t]]$score, na.rm = TRUE),
                     numeric(1)),
  coverage = vapply(taxa, function(t) mean(sc[[t]]$in_interval,
                                           na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

```{r score-numbers, include = FALSE}
inside <- sum(vapply(taxa, function(t) sum(sc[[t]]$in_interval,
                                           na.rm = TRUE), numeric(1)))
scored <- sum(vapply(taxa, function(t) sum(!is.na(sc[[t]]$score)),
                     numeric(1)))
```

Of the `r scored` observations in 1994, `r inside` fell inside their
90% intervals, close to the coverage the intervals claim. The CRPS
compares models scored on the same data, such as this VAR against an
independent autoregression for each taxon. The
[forecast evaluation article](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/forecast_evaluation.html)
works through that comparison with leave-future-out
cross-validation.

The plankton of Lake Washington rise and fall mostly with the seasons
and with phosphorus. In this fit, `r n_clear` of the twenty lagged
interactions among the taxa separate from zero. The community damps a perturbation within a season. The
forecasts for the held-out year keep close to their stated
coverage.

## Where to next

Each function used here has a help page, such as `?irf` or
`?residual_cor`, with its arguments and output. `how_to_cite()`
writes a methods paragraph for a fitted model, with its references.

Related articles:

- [Hierarchical VARs](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/hierarchical_var.html)
  fit one VAR per group of series, such as one per lake. Each group's
  $A$ and $\Sigma$ are drawn towards a shared mean.
- [Dynamic factor models](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/dfm.html)
  describe many series with fewer latent processes than series.
- [Forecast evaluation](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/forecast_evaluation.html)
  covers scoring rules and leave-future-out cross-validation.
- [mvgam overview](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/mvgam_overview.html)
  introduces the observation and trend formulas.
- [Formatting data](https://nicholasjclark.github.io/mvgam/articles/data.html)
  covers the long data format and `mvgam_data()`.

Chapter 8 of the
[Applied Time Series Analysis](https://atsa-es.github.io/atsa-labs/chap-msscov.html)
lab book fits multivariate autoregressive state-space models to the
same Lake Washington plankton with MARSS.
